$comment: Organs are countable modules, not flags. Count comes from the body's own symmetry and segmentation, so three eyes is a thing a body can be rather than a special case someone wrote.

organs.why: A patch of pigment and a shadow. No image, only direction and day length. The floor of vision and available to a single cell.
Invaginate the patch and you get direction without optics. Every step from here to a lens eye is uphill in fitness the whole way, which is why eyes are cheap to evolve and expensive to keep.
Nautilus. Real imaging, terrible light budget — resolution and brightness trade directly against aperture with no lens to break the tie.
Breaks the aperture/resolution trade. Costs a nervous system that can use it — which is why the nervous axis gates it and why an eye on a body with a nerve net is wasted tissue.
Resolution scales with the number of ommatidia, so acuity costs volume linearly instead of quadratically — an eye that only makes sense on a body that is already wearing its skeleton.

Guanine reflector instead of a lens — scallops and lobsters. Wins wherever the medium's refractive index is close to the tissue's, which is most of the ocean, and it is the right answer in any solvent where a lens cannot bend light.

The only honest microwave eye. Beat the 1.22 lambda over D limit by making D the whole animal: a line of receptors along the segments, phase-compared by a brain that can do it. Needs a body metres across, which is why it is gated on size class 8 and up.
Pit viper. Thermal difference, millikelvin sensitivity, angular resolution of a few degrees at best because it is a pinhole in the far field of a long wavelength.
Jelly-filled canals reading microvolts per centimetre. Free imaging in the dark, in a conductor, at body-length range — and useless the moment the lineage leaves the water.
Flow imaging along the flank. The cheapest way to see a moving body in an opaque fluid.
A dense grain in a hair-lined sac. Down, and how fast down is changing.
Crystal chains aligned to the field. Worth nothing on a world with no dynamo.
The first sense. Gradient following works at any body size and in any solvent.
A membrane matched to the medium's impedance. In a dense atmosphere it hears further than an eye sees.
Active imaging. The correct sense on any world where the photon budget is zero — under ice, at depth, or on the night side of a locked planet.
Stacked cells as a battery. Once you can read a field it costs little to make one, which is why electrogenesis follows electroreception rather than the reverse.
Make your own photons where there are none. Counter-illumination, lure, and alarm — three unrelated jobs, one organ.
A hard edge that closes. On a radial body it comes in `symmetryOrder` pieces — five teeth around a mouth, which is Aristotle's lantern.
A rasping belt. Grazes films off rock, which is the largest food source on any young planet.
Sieve the water. The single most common feeding solution in the ocean and the one that gets a body to whale size.
Chemistry instead of force. Cheap for a small body, which is why it is how small things kill large things.
Neutral buoyancy for free. Fails above a depth-dependent pressure, so the deep sea uses lipid instead.
Separating the pumps is what lets pressure differ between the gas exchanger and the body, and that is the precondition for high aerobic scope.
The same trick used for oxygen, for heat and for salt. Turns a gradient into a gain and it is why a gill can pull 80% of the oxygen from water that holds almost none.
Negative power cost — the organ pays. Chemosynthetic trophosome, coral zooxanthellae, a rumen. Endosymbiosis is the cheapest new metabolism a body can acquire because it does not have to invent it.
Antifreeze glycoproteins. Turns a lethal isotherm into a habitable one, and it is what makes a cryobrine habitat reachable at all.
Survive the interval. On a world with violent climate swings this is worth more than any organ that improves the good years.
